title: Slide 1 · Capstone: auditing a hospital teaching-room handoff
question: A staff note and a scan both concern ticket T40. The note records a check at minute 6 and the scan records a handoff at minute 9. Assuming the note is accepted as evidence, which event came first and by how much?
answer: The recorded check came first by three minutes. Both rows refer to T40, so the time comparison concerns one handoff.

title: Slide 2 · Translate the clerk’s question into a rule
question: A check note for T18 also mentions projector P7. May the clerk use it to clear T17?
answer: The projector can be borrowed several times. T17 needs a check record tied to its own handoff. The shared item name cannot establish that link.

title: Slide 3 · Connect a learned signal to an evidence record
question: If a note only promises a future check but receives 0.93, what can the rule establish?
answer: It can establish that the classifier admitted that note. The wording does not document a completed check. A clerk who examines the source can catch the classification error.

title: Slide 4 · Return a finding the clerk can inspect
question: What would you write for the clerk, and what could the clerk check?
answer: “For T17, candidate note K8 reports a check at minute 12. Scan H4 records a handoff at minute 18. The recorded order meets the teaching-room rule.” The clerk can verify the note wording, times and ticket IDs.

title: Slide 5 · Run the audit on three tickets
question: What would make this submission convincing beyond matching the three printed labels?
answer: For each decision, explain what the score test and time test contributed, cite the available records and name any missing evidence. Test a new case such as a high score with tied timestamps. Check that the clerk can see the uncertainty.

title: Slide 6 · Trace ticket T17 back to both sources
question: Replace this line: scan_id, handoff = "H4", 18 with: scan_id, handoff = "H4", 12 What will print?
answer:
T17 needs review K8 H4
Both observations now carry minute 12. The recorded times do not establish which event came first, and the report retains both source IDs for review.

title: Slide 8 · What your audit can support
question: A second reviewer reproduces an “in order” result, then learns that the qualifying note’s minute was its filing time, not its event time. What should appear in the audit now?
answer: Record the discovered assumption and mark the order for review until the actual check time is available. Reproducing the computation shows how the first label arose, but the available times no longer establish the sequence.

title: Office hours · Where is the neurosymbolic part of this capstone?
question: Where is the neurosymbolic part of this capstone?
answer: The learned classifier proposes what free-text notes mean. The symbolic part checks explicit conditions about ticket identity, admissible evidence and time order. An error can arise in either part. Keeping the note and scan IDs lets a reviewer test the particular decision.

title: Office hours · How does this relate to healthcare decision support?
question: How does this relate to healthcare decision support?
answer: Both an administrative audit and a clinical compliance study can ask what a record supports under an explicit rule. This projector exercise lets you practice representing evidence and uncertainty. Interpreting patient-care protocols requires clinical expertise, validated definitions and evaluation on appropriate data.

title: Office hours · What should I hand in for the capstone?
question: What should I hand in for the capstone?
answer: Submit runnable code, a trace for each supplied ticket, the predicted and observed outcomes for your two added tests, and a short error analysis of the four independently reviewed tickets in the final exercise. A reader should be able to reproduce each label and locate its supporting records.

title: Exercise 1
question: Build the capstone review for T17, T18 and T19. Report each status with its source IDs and explain the tests in everyday language.
answer: T17 is in order on the records: K8 scores 0.92 and reports minute 12 before H4 at 18. T18 is reversed: K9 scores 0.90 but reports 20 after H5 at 17. T19 needs review: K12 scores 0.55 and there is no scan. Its evidence cannot establish the order.

title: Exercise 2
question: Add a ticket that isolates the cutoff boundary and one that isolates equal times. Predict both outputs before running your program.
answer: Try T20, K13, 0.80, 7, H6, 8. The inclusive cutoff admits K13 and the result is in order. Try T21, K14, 0.95, 9, H7, 9. The note passes, but minute-level times tie, so the result is needs review.

title: Exercise 3
question: A clerk independently labels four new tickets: in order, reversed, needs review, needs review. The system gives in order, in order, needs review, in order. Evaluate it and propose one diagnostic step.
answer: Two of four labels agree. The second ticket is a missed reversal. The fourth is an unsupported clearance. Inspect source IDs, wording and timestamps for each, replay the cutoff and order tests, and report which step first diverged from the clerk’s evidence. For a new version, keep fresh cases for independent evaluation.

title: Lab case 1 · Event time reversed
question: Which finding and which evidence should the desk display?
answer: Reversed. Candidate note K20 reports a check at 17, after the handoff in H20 at 14. A clerk can inspect those records before drawing conclusions about the actual handoff.

title: Lab case 2 · Check without a scan
question: How should this differ from a documented reversal?
answer: Needs review. K21 is a candidate check record, but the missing handoff time prevents ordering the events. Show K21 and the missing scan.

title: Lab case 3 · A misleading high score
question: What does the program print, and what should a reviewer do?
answer: It labels T27 in order because the score passes and 9 is earlier than 12. The note itself describes unfinished work. Flag the note classification, record the correction and send the ticket for review.
